Headless CMS vs WordPress

When does going headless make sense?

A plain-English guide for marketing teams and founders.

What “headless” means

One job, not two.

WordPress stores your content and renders the site with a theme. A headless CMS only manages content. Your website, app or any other “head” pulls it through an API.

Side by side
01Page speed: theme-dependent vs typically very fast
02Design: limited by the theme vs complete freedom
03Security: public admin vs editor kept separate
04Channels: website-first vs site, apps and more
05Plugins: huge ecosystem vs built or integrated

WordPress is enough when
✓It’s mostly a blog or a handful of pages
✓You rely on plugins for forms, SEO or shop
✓You have no developer for layout changes
✓Speed is fine after caching and image work

Headless pays off when
→Speed matters for revenue: e-commerce, leads, paid traffic
→Design is a differentiator: 3D, scrollytelling
→You publish to a website and an app
→Plugin upkeep has become a recurring cost

Popular options
01Sanity: custom editing studio
02Strapi, Payload: open source, self-hostable
03Contentful: managed, enterprise workflows
04Storyblok: visual editor
05Headless WordPress: keep the admin you know

What about SEO?

Headless doesn’t hurt SEO when the front-end outputs real HTML (server rendering or static generation).

The real risks: client-only rendering and lost URLs in migration. Fix with 301 redirects, preserved metadata and generated sitemaps.
